items.en: Why the Breath Comes First: Āryadeva's Teaching
items.zh: 初禪 · 明修習 · 料揀

zh: 復次，提婆初出世時，伏外道已，諸人信敬，度人出家，不可稱數。於是大集在家、出家七眾弟子及剎利、婆羅門等，大眾之中，昇師子座，淚下如雨。爾時，大眾皆悉默念：「將非佛法欲滅，外道復興邪？將非國大擾亂，疫病流行邪？」菩薩爾時知大眾心念，以白㲲巾拭淚，更整容服，舉右手而言：「亦非佛法欲滅，外道將興，非國不安，疫病流行，但傷佛日潛輝，賢聖月沒，袈裟之中空無所有耳。」于時大眾聞此語已，各自感傷，發聲大哭。爾時，飛鳥雜類在虛空中，繽紛亂墜，皆悉悲鳴。
en: Furthermore: when Āryadeva first appeared in the world, having already subdued the non-Buddhist teachers, people everywhere came to believe in and revere him, and those he brought across into the monastic life were beyond counting. At one point, a great assembly gathered — lay and ordained disciples of the seven assemblies, together with kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others — and, in the midst of this great assembly, he ascended the lion's seat, and tears fell from him like rain. At that moment, the whole assembly silently wondered: "Could it be that the Buddhadharma is about to be extinguished, and the non-Buddhist paths about to flourish again? Or could it be that the kingdom is about to fall into great turmoil, plague and pestilence about to spread?"

The bodhisattva, knowing at once what was in the assembly's mind, wiped away his tears with a white cotton cloth, straightened his robes and bearing, raised his right hand, and said: "Neither is the Buddhadharma about to be extinguished, nor are the non-Buddhist paths about to flourish; neither is the kingdom about to fall into unrest, nor is plague about to spread. I grieve only that the sun of the Buddha has already set beneath the horizon, that the moon of the sages and noble ones has already sunk from view, and that, within these very monastic robes gathered here, there is, in truth, nothing left within them at all."

Upon hearing these words, the whole assembly, each moved to sorrow, wept aloud together. At that moment, the birds and various creatures in the open sky scattered and fell in confusion, all crying out in grief as well.

zh:
爾時，菩薩以慈軟音安慰大眾，而說偈言：
佛日常在世，無目不見耳，
賢聖月不沒，障礙故不見。
若能淨膚翳，當自得覩見，
何為沒憂海，癡醉如嬰兒？
爾時，大眾聞菩薩慈音，心各醒悟，攝心安坐，寂然無聲，諦觀菩薩，咸欲聞法。爾時，菩薩普告大眾而說偈言：
佛說甘露門，名阿那波那，
於諸法門中，第一安隱道。
因緣次第起，不雜諸妄想，
譬如種石榴，芽莖次第生。
華實及色味，自然非可作，
時至時自證，非如脂粉色。
汝等調熟地，惠汝石榴種，
令心入甘露，道法次第生。
en:
The bodhisattva then, with a voice gentle and full of compassion, consoled the assembly, speaking this verse:
"The sun of the Buddha forever remains in the world; it is only the eyeless who fail to see it.
The moon of the sages and noble ones has never truly set; it is only obstruction that keeps it from view.
Should you cleanse away the film clouding your own eyes, you would see it for yourselves at once —
Why, then, sink into an ocean of grief, deluded and drunk like a newborn child?"
At that, the assembly, hearing the bodhisattva's compassionate voice, each awakened in mind, gathered themselves, and sat down in peace, still and silent, gazing intently at the bodhisattva, all wishing to hear the Dharma. The bodhisattva then addressed the whole assembly, speaking this verse:
"The Buddha spoke of the gate to the deathless, named ānāpāna —
Among every dharma-gate whatsoever, it is the foremost path to peace and stability.
It arises through causes and conditions in due sequence, unmixed with any deluded thought,
Just as a planted pomegranate seed sends up its sprout and stem in due sequence.
Its flowers, fruit, and their color and flavor arise naturally, not something that can be forced —
When the time comes, one bears witness to it oneself; it is not like applying rouge or powder to the skin.
You who have properly cultivated this ground — I now bestow on you the pomegranate's own seed,
That your minds may enter the deathless, the dharma of the path arising in due sequence."

zh: 從此以來，西國法師相傳不絕，多以此法為學道之初。若四依大士、六通菩薩說法度人，此為首唱，豈非入道初門？末代相承，說法教授自不修禪，既無內道，出言即便破人修定，若觀提婆之說，乃以禪定為要。世人顛倒，實可哀哉！復有人言：「禪法一向不得處眾說之。」敬尋提婆在大眾中廣說禪定，今時豈頓杜口？但不得言：「我證是法，某證是法，及禪祕密微妙境界。」向人說此，獲罪不輕。
en: From this time onward, the teacher-masters of the Western Lands have transmitted this without interruption, for the most part taking this very method as the starting point of study on the path. If even the great beings of the four reliances and the bodhisattvas possessing the six supernormal powers, take this as their own opening proclamation when expounding the Dharma to liberate others, how could it not be the very first gate into the path?

In this latter age, those who inherit the transmission and teach the Dharma to others, without cultivating dhyāna themselves, having no inward path of their own, speak out and thereby only destroy others' own cultivation of concentration instead. Looking at what Āryadeva himself taught, dhyāna-concentration is precisely what is essential — the inverted state of people in this world is truly something to lament! There are, further, those who say: "The dharma of dhyāna should, without exception, never be expounded before an assembly at all." But respectfully examining Āryadeva's own example — expounding dhyāna-concentration at length before a great assembly — how, then, could one simply close one's mouth entirely in the present age? One should simply avoid saying: "I myself have realized this dharma," or "So-and-so has realized this dharma," or speaking of dhyāna's own secret and subtle states to others — to speak of these things to another incurs no small offense.

This story of Āryadeva's grief — mourning not any external catastrophe but the hollowness beneath the robes of a Saṅgha that has stopped actually practicing — reframes everything the treatise has spent four fascicles building as urgent rather than merely thorough. The pomegranate simile, from Āryadeva's own verse as Zhiyi quotes it, captures something this whole treatise has insisted on from its opening pages: realization cannot be forced or faked (its color comes forth naturally, "not like applying rouge or powder to the skin") — it can only be cultivated in proper sequence and witnessed for oneself when its own time comes. The closing rule about never claiming personal attainment, sandwiched between two passages defending the public teaching of dhyāna, draws a precise line: teach the method as fully and publicly as Āryadeva did, but never claim the result — a distinction the treatise clearly regards as being violated more in its own era than observed.

items.en: The First Dhyāna: Marks of Realization

zh: 第三、明證禪相，通方便論證自有三階：一、證欲界定相；二、證未到定相；三、正明證初禪相。一、明證欲界定，自有二意：一、正明證相；二、明得失。今說欲界中自有三：一、麁住心；二、細住心；三、證欲界定。一、麁住相者，因前息道諸方便修習，心漸虛凝，不復緣慮，名為麁住。細住相者，於後其心泯泯轉細，即是細住心。當得此麁細住時，或將得時，必有持身法起。此法發時，身心自然正直，坐不疲倦，如物持身，若好持身，但微微扶助身力而已。若是麁持身者，堅急勁強，來則苦急堅強，去則寬緩困人。此非好法。心既細已，於覺心自然明淨，與定相應，定法持心，任運不動，從淺入深，或經一坐，無分散意，所以說此名欲界定。入此定時，欲界報身相未盡故。
en: Third, clarifying the marks of realizing dhyāna: discussing realization broadly, together with the expedient means, this itself has three stages — the mark of realizing desire-realm concentration; the mark of realizing the "not-yet-arrived" concentration; and directly clarifying the mark of realizing the first dhyāna.

First, clarifying the realization of desire-realm concentration: this itself has two parts — directly clarifying its mark, and clarifying its gain and loss. Here, within the desire realm, three stages are given: the mind coarsely settling; the mind finely settling; and the realization of desire-realm concentration proper.

As for the mark of coarse settling: through the various expedient means of the path of the breath already cultivated, the mind gradually grows empty and fixed, no longer chasing after objects of thought — this is called coarse settling. As for the mark of fine settling: afterward, the mind grows ever more indistinct and refined — this is precisely the fine-settling mind. Upon reaching this coarse or fine settling, or as one is about to reach it, a body-sustaining phenomenon is bound to arise. When this phenomenon arises, body and mind become naturally upright, sitting without fatigue, as though something were sustaining the body — and, when this sustaining is proper, it merely, faintly, lends support to the body's own strength. But if it is a coarse form of body-sustaining instead, it is rigid, tense, and forceful — arriving with a strained, forced rigidity, and departing leaving the body slack and exhausted; this is not the proper phenomenon.

Once the mind has grown fine, the awakened mind itself becomes naturally bright and pure, according with concentration; the dharma of concentration then sustains the mind, unmoved of its own accord, proceeding from the shallow into the deep — sometimes throughout an entire sitting, with no thought of it scattering at all. This is why this state is called desire-realm concentration: upon entering this concentration, the marks of the desire realm's own retributive body have not yet been entirely exhausted.

zh: 二、明得失者，入欲界定，法心既淺，未有支持，難得易失。易失因緣，是事須識。失定有二種：一、從外緣失，謂得定時，不善用心，內外方便，中途違犯，則退失禪定。復次，若行者當得定時，或向人說，或現定相，令他知覺，或卒有事緣相壞，如是等種種外事，於中不覺不識，障法既生，則便失定。若能將護，本得不失，障不得生，故名為得。二者、約內論得失者，有六種法能失禪定：一、希望心；二、疑心；三、驚怖；四、大喜；五、重愛；六、憂悔。未得禪有一，謂希望心。入禪有四，謂疑、怖、喜、愛。出禪多有憂悔，此則能破定心令退失。若通論此六，皆得在未入住出中。俱有此六法，能退失定；若能離此六法，即易得定。以不失故，名得也。此雖近事，若不說者，則人不知。若善取其意，則知遮障。
en: Second, clarifying gain and loss: upon entering desire-realm concentration, the mind of this dharma is still shallow, not yet sustained by any factor, and so is difficult to attain and easy to lose. The causes and conditions of this easy loss are matters one must recognize. Loss of concentration is of two kinds.

First, loss through an external condition: this means that, at the very time concentration is attained, the mind is applied improperly, some fault is committed partway through in the external or internal expedient means, and dhyāna-concentration thereby regresses and is lost. Furthermore: if the practitioner, at the very moment of attaining concentration, either speaks of it to others, or displays some outward sign of concentration so that others become aware of it, or some sudden matter or condition arises and disrupts it — such various external matters as these, if not recognized and understood within, allow the obstructing dharma to arise, and concentration is thereupon lost. If one is able to guard and protect it properly, what has already been attained is not lost, and no obstruction is allowed to arise — hence this is called "attaining" it.

Second, discussing gain and loss in terms of internal causes: there are six kinds of dharma able to cause the loss of dhyāna-concentration — a mind of expectation; a mind of doubt; fright; great joy; excessive attachment; and worry and regret. Before dhyāna is attained, there is one of these: a mind of expectation. Upon entering dhyāna, there are four: doubt, fright, joy, and attachment. Upon emerging from dhyāna, worry and regret are frequently present — and these are able to break apart the concentrated mind, causing it to regress and be lost. Speaking of these six generally, they may all occur before entering, while abiding within, or upon emerging from concentration alike; wherever any of these six dharmas is present, concentration is liable to regress and be lost; and if one is able to remain free of these six dharmas, concentration is thereby easily attained. Because it is thus not lost, this is called "attaining" it. Although this may seem a minor matter, if it were not explained, people would have no way of knowing it; properly grasping its sense, one comes to recognize the obstruction itself.

zh: 二、明證未到地定相，因此欲界定後，身心泯然虛豁，失於欲界之身，坐中不見頭手床敷，猶若虛空，此是未到地定。所言未到地者，此地能生初禪故，即是初禪方便定，亦名未來禪，亦名忽然湛心。證此定時，不無淺深之相，今不具明。復次，此等定中，或有邪偽，行者應證，其相非一，略出二事：一、定心過明；二者、過暗。並是邪定。明者，入定時見外境界青、黃、赤、白，或見日月星辰、宮殿等事，或一時日乃至七日不出禪定，見一切事，如得神通，此為邪，當急去之。二者、若入此定，暗忽無所覺知，如眠熟不異，即是無心想法，能令行人生顛倒心，當急却之。此則略說邪定之相，是中妨難，非可具以文傳。復次，若依《成論》、《毘曇》分別二定，為不便也。今依尊者瞿沙所明分別二定有異，亦應無失。具如前引《摩訶衍》中釋，而多見坐人證定之時，實有兩種定相不同，是故今說欲界、未到二定各異。
en: Second, clarifying the mark of realizing the "not-yet-arrived" concentration: following this desire-realm concentration, body and mind become indistinct and vacantly open, the sense of the desire-realm body itself lost — while sitting, one no longer sees one's own head, hands, or the seat beneath, as though it were all empty space. This is the "not-yet-arrived" concentration. As for what is meant by "not-yet-arrived": this stage is able to give rise to the first dhyāna, and so is precisely the first dhyāna's own preliminary concentration — also called the future dhyāna, and also called the mind suddenly grown clear. When this concentration is realized, it is not without its own marks of shallowness and depth, though these are not given in full detail here.

Furthermore: within concentrations such as these, there may also be deviance and falsity present, which the practitioner should be able to recognize; its marks are not of one kind only, though, in brief, two matters are given: the concentrated mind being excessively bright; and being excessively dark — both of these are deviant concentration. As for excessive brightness: upon entering concentration, one sees external states of blue, yellow, red, and white, or sees the sun, moon, and stars, or palaces and other such things, or, for a full day or even as long as seven days, fails to emerge from dhyāna-concentration, seeing all manner of things as though one had attained supernormal powers — this is deviant, and one should urgently rid oneself of it. As for excessive darkness: if, upon entering this concentration, one becomes dark and dull, aware of nothing at all, no different from being deeply asleep — this is precisely a state without any mental activity at all, able to cause the practitioner to give rise to an inverted mind; one should urgently repel this as well. This, in brief, describes the marks of deviant concentration; the difficulties involved cannot be conveyed in full through writing.

Furthermore: were one to follow the Satyasiddhi-śāstra or the Abhidharma in distinguishing these two concentrations, this would not prove convenient here. Here, instead, the distinction between these two concentrations as clarified by the Venerable Ghoṣa is followed, which should likewise be without fault — exactly as already cited above from the Mahāyāna treatise's own explanation. And, having observed many practitioners at the actual moment of realizing concentration, there are, in truth, two genuinely differing marks of concentration present — hence desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" concentration are here said to be each distinct from the other.

The body-sustaining phenomenon and the coarse/fine settling distinction give a concrete physical criterion for a state that could otherwise only be described introspectively — a genuinely settled sitting posture feels sustained rather than held, "as though something were sustaining the body," and a forced, rigid posture is diagnosed here as itself a sign the mind has not actually settled yet. The six causes of losing concentration (expectation before, doubt/fright/joy/attachment upon entering, worry and regret upon emerging) are worth comparing with the ten pairs of wrong marks from fascicle 3: both are diagnostic lists built from ordinary, recognizable mental events rather than exotic experiences, on the theory that what derails practice is usually mundane. The excessive-brightness and excessive-darkness deviant marks also echo fascicle 3's own "明闇" pair from the ten wrong marks almost exactly — the same diagnostic returning at a new stage of practice.

quiz.q: Āryadeva wept before the great assembly. Why, by his own account?
options: the Dharma was ending and non-Buddhists rising
grieving that the Buddha's sun had set, the moon of the sages sunk, and within the robes there was nothing at all
quiz.why: "Neither is the Buddhadharma about to be extinguished ... I grieve only that the sun of the Buddha has already set beneath the horizon, that the moon of the sages and noble ones has already sunk from view, and that, within these very monastic robes gathered here, there is, in truth, nothing left within them at all." The other options were the assembly's guesses.

quiz.q: In Āryadeva's verse on ānāpāna, what illustrates realization coming "when the time comes"?
options: a pomegranate seed whose sprout, flower, fruit, and flavor arise in sequence naturally, not like rouge or powder
quiz.why: "It arises through causes and conditions in due sequence ... Just as a planted pomegranate seed sends up its sprout and stem in due sequence. Its flowers, fruit, and their color and flavor arise naturally, not something that can be forced — When the time comes, one bears witness to it oneself; it is not like applying rouge or powder to the skin."

quiz.q: Some say the dharma of dhyāna should never be taught before an assembly. What is the text's view?
options: Āryadeva taught dhyāna at length before an assembly, so why stay silent? Only do not say "I have realized this" or "so-and-so has," or speak of dhyāna's secret states
quiz.why: "Respectfully examining Āryadeva's own example — expounding dhyāna-concentration at length before a great assembly — how, then, could one simply close one's mouth entirely in the present age? One should simply avoid saying: 'I myself have realized this dharma,' or 'So-and-so has realized this dharma,' or speaking of dhyāna's own secret and subtle states to others."

quiz.q: Within desire-realm concentration, which three stages are given?
options: coarse settling, fine settling, realizing desire-realm concentration
quiz.why: "Here, within the desire realm, three stages are given: the mind coarsely settling; the mind finely settling; and the realization of desire-realm concentration proper."

quiz.q: Of the six internal dharmas that cause loss of concentration, how are they distributed before, upon entering, and upon emerging?
options: before: expectation; entering: doubt, fright, joy, attachment; emerging: worry and regret
quiz.why: "There are six kinds of dharma able to cause the loss of dhyāna-concentration — a mind of expectation; a mind of doubt; fright; great joy; excessive attachment; and worry and regret. Before dhyāna is attained, there is one of these: a mind of expectation. Upon entering dhyāna, there are four: doubt, fright, joy, and attachment. Upon emerging from dhyāna, worry and regret are frequently present."

quiz.q: What is the realization of the not-yet-arrived concentration like, and what else is it called?
options: body and mind vacantly open, the desire-realm body lost, not seeing head, hands, or seat, like empty space; also called the future dhyāna and the suddenly deepened mind
quiz.why: "Body and mind become indistinct and vacantly open, the sense of the desire-realm body itself lost — while sitting, one no longer sees one's own head, hands, or the seat beneath, as though it were all empty space ... also called the future dhyāna, and also called the suddenly deepened mind."

quiz.q: What two kinds of deviant concentration in the not-yet-arrived state does the text give?
options: excessively bright (seeing colors, sun, palaces, as if with powers) and excessively dark (dull, aware of nothing, like deep sleep)
quiz.why: "In brief, two matters are given: the concentrated mind being excessively bright; and being excessively dark — both of these are deviant concentration ... seeing all manner of things as though one had attained supernormal powers — this is deviant ... if, upon entering this concentration, one becomes dark and dull, aware of nothing at all, no different from being deeply asleep."
